claims.claim: Siepmann's 2017 corpus study: the impression of archaicity comes from overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words (yonder, journey (v), topmost), avoidance of modern-world words, and dense use of coinages, unusual patterns and obsolescent words; reference corpora were 30m (19th-c fiction), 160m (post-war fiction) and 94m (mixed).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)

claims.claim: Modern key words (they, big, wake, wall, tired, smoke) are used in nineteenth-century patterns, e.g. 'a black smoke' with indefinite article, rare in modern fiction.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)

claims.claim: Wikipedia cites Turner: Tolkien's style is generally simple parataxis, varied by the race and standing of the speaker; at Pelennor the paratactic repeated 'and' creates an exalted biblical register with few archaic words.

Wikipedia cites Shippey's 'loose semantic fit' (conjunctions avoiding explicit logical connection) at significant moments and Rosebury on inversion working better than the plain order ('But glad would he have been').

McIntosh, citing Garth (p. 271), describes Tolkien's parataxis as short simple sentences joined by 'and' in the Ride of the Rohirrim and Pelennor, producing breathless excitement and rising foreboding.
claims.source: Jonathan McIntosh, 'Tolkien's use of parataxis', The Flame Imperishable (2012)

claims.claim: Thomas (per Nepveu): The Hobbit opens with a very intrusive narrator who recedes as the book grows serious; the LOTR narrator is impartial and self-effacing, and early LOTR drafts were unsuccessful returns to the intrusive voice (Booth's scale).
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, summary of Paul Edmund Thomas, 'Some of Tolkien's Narrators' (2000)

claims.claim: Poveda: The Hobbit's narrator is omniscient, comments on events, addresses the reader as a child, withholds and anticipates information, and is conscious of the written medium.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)

claims.claim: Poveda: LOTR begins in a conversational tone with Hobbit-style asides and an occasionally unreliable narrator ('probably started by the knowledgeable Sam'), but as the plot progresses the voice becomes neutral and the narrator disappears behind the characters.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)
claims.quote: the narrator disappears behind the characters

claims.feature: archaic style confined to elf/men episodes
claims.claim: Poveda: archaic forms (ye, hath) and noun-adjective inversion are not predominant but confined to episodes of Elves and Men inspired by epic, chiefly Books II and III; capitalised common nouns (the Sea, the City) mark the style.
claims.source: Jaume Albero Poveda, 'Narrative models in Tolkien's stories of Middle-earth', Journal of English Studies 4 (2003-04)

claims.claim: Litschko, using Stanzel and Booth, characterises The Hobbit's narrator as an intrusive authorial narrator who comments and judges, addresses readers directly, shifts point of view, and changes tone in the later-written final chapters.
claims.source: Nadja Litschko, 'The Voice of the Narrator in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit' (GRIN, 2006)

claims.feature: limited omniscience when no hobbit present
claims.claim: aefenglommung: the story is seen mainly through Frodo's mind, occasionally Merry or Pippin, and increasingly Sam; where no hobbit is present Tolkien draws back into limited omniscience and we do not enter Aragorn's, Gimli's or Legolas's minds, Book 3 reading like a stage-play.
claims.quote: we do not enter their minds

claims.feature: multiple tellers and limited vs omniscient narrators
claims.claim: Barkley compares the versions of tales told by Bilbo, Aragorn, Gandalf, the Red Book's scholar-editor and the Silmarillion's omniscient narrator: the limited narrator is narrower in scope but richer in detail, dialogue and song, the omniscient broader in theme.
claims.source: Christine Barkley, 'Point of View in Tolkien', Mythlore 21.2 (1996)
claims.quote: The limited third-person narrative focuses attention more on one character

claims.claim: Barkley: the Prologue's Red Book of Westmarch frame authenticates the tale, gives away the happy ending, and contrasts with The Hobbit, whose narrator paraphrased Bilbo's account and revealed his own bias.
claims.source: Christine Barkley, 'Point of View in Tolkien', Mythlore 21.2 (1996)

claims.claim: Wikipedia cites Thomson (1967) and Turner (2011) for the found-manuscript frame in which Tolkien poses as editor/translator of the Red Book, with genealogies and footnotes as editorial apparatus.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Tauber: The Hobbit's 19 chapters (70th Anniversary edition) yield 95,137 whitespace tokens in 11,532 types, or 95,390/95,643 depending on em-dash handling; 5,165 types carry trailing punctuation and 254 contain em-dashes.
claims.source: James Tauber, 'Tokenizing the Hobbit' (Digital Tolkien Project, 2021)
